searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's; one left unspent. Two were shared: the consorzio's disciplinare for the release rule of all five records, and the consorzio's history for the dates every record leans on (1865 and 1869, the DOC of 1966, the consorzio of 1967, the DOCG of 1980). Eleven were restricted to a primary body's or a house's own domain (the consorzio twice, biondisanti.it three times, tenutailpoggione.it twice, banfi.it three times, casanovadineri.it twice, soldera.it once) and are read as primary through their summaries. One search for Teodolinda Banfi without a domain returned nothing on the subject and was repeated with the house's domain. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; nothing that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the release rule (it touches every record), then to the dates, the people, the sites and the making; a fact the Codex library states stood on the library unless a search contradicted it.

Where two of the house's own pages, or the house and the trade, disagreed (Banfi's aspect, Soldera's temperature control, Casanova di Neri's cask months), the record now says only what both allow, or nothing.
Sources whose address or title carries a writer's name (a critic's site on Soldera's departure, a writer's wine wiki on Soldera and Casanova di Neri) were read in the results but never cited.

tested: The release rule: the disciplinare releases Brunello on 1 January of the year after the fifth year counted from the harvest, six for a Riserva, with two years at least in wood and four months in bottle, six for a Riserva: the record's six years before release was loose and is set right.

Clemente Santi, the 1865 vintage and its silver medal of 1869 from the agrarian committee of Montepulciano, his grandson Ferruccio, the 1888 as the first wine officially labelled Brunello di Montalcino, the DOC of 1966, the consorzio of 1967, the DOCG of 1980 and the consorzio's claim that it was Italy's first: confirmed on the consorzio's own pages. The consorzio calls Clemente a chemist; pharmacist rested on one source and was cut.
Ferruccio's death in 1917: the importer, Opening a Bottle and other trade profiles give 1917; a wine glossary gives 1848 to 1916. Kept, and left open.
The topping up and recorking of the 1888 in 1927, 1970 and 1985 and BBS11 registered in 1978: confirmed on the estate's own 1888 and 1891 sheets.

The making: the estate's 2016 Riserva sheet gives upright Slavonian oak vats, indigenous yeasts selected in its own vineyards and three years in Slavonian oak; its general Riserva page gives cement vats. The record names the 2016 sheet, so it stands, with the conflict left open.

The sites: the estate's 1995 Riserva sheet gives 300 to 500 metres, every aspect from south to north, stony soils of mixed origin with galestro the best; the Rosso 2019 sheet places Greppo south east of the town; the wine page gives the Riserva's vines over twenty five years. Around 500 metres, clay and marl were changed.
The grandson's death in 2013 and the sale to EPI at the end of 2016: on the author's sources, not contradicted.
The house rules: the living descendants are described (people.json holds Tancredi Biondi Santi), no price or score, British spelling, no dash.

Vigna Paganelli planted in 1964 on an alluvial terrace: the estate's Riserva page for the year, and two merchants for the alluvial terrace or plateau; confirmed.

The making: the estate's 2020 sheet gives a submerged cap fermentation of fifteen to twenty days in steel with indigenous yeasts, the malolactic in steel and long ageing in French oak casks of 30 to 50 hectolitres; the three years rest on Decanter and a merchant: confirmed, the length left open.
The sites: the sheet gives the oldest vineyards between 150 and 450 metres and the estate about ten kilometres south of Montalcino: confirmed.
The release rule on the label set right from the disciplinare.

tested: The firm and its name: founded in New York in 1919 by most accounts (one says 1917) and named for the founder's aunt, who kept the house of the Milan cardinal who became Pius XI; the house's own site says she was the first lay person to head a pope's household staff: the record tells it as the family does, and she is described, her dates not found.
Riunite from 1969: on the author's Decanter profile and Wikipedia, not contradicted.

The founding in 1978 (the first land and the first Sangiovese planted that year) and the winery's opening on 12 September 1984: confirmed on the house's own pages. The castle in 1983 stays as the estate's timeline, hedged.
The credit for launching Brunello in the United States: the house's own news page gives it to one of the brothers, as the record says.

Poggio all'Oro: first vintage 1985 and made only in great vintages, on the house's sheets; the altitude 229 to 250 metres on its vineyard sheet; the soil brown clay and silt with calcareous stones and pebbles on its sheets, sandy clay loam on its new site; the aspect north west on the new site and south west in a 2004 release: the aspect cut.

The making: a 2007 sheet names that vintage as the first in Horizon tanks, so the start of 2010 was wrong or unsettled and is cut; the 2016 sheet gives 80 per cent in 60 and 90 hectolitre casks and 20 in 350 litre barrels for thirty months at least, the 2015 forty two months at 70 and 30: the record's from 2015 confirmed.
The service at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: the house's own Poggio all'Oro site.
The questions: the distractor a river terrace beside the Orcia could be read as right, since the house calls the site a broad natural terrace and the estate lies by the Orcia; it is replaced.
The house rules: the brothers, the next generation and the oenologist who found the land are described; no price or score; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The dates: founded in 1971 in the east of Montalcino, the first Brunello, the White Label, from 1978, Cerretalto first bottled in 1981, the estate handed to the son in 1991 and Tenuta Nuova first made in 1993: confirmed on the estate's own pages and a producer guide.

Cerretalto: a four hectare natural amphitheatre above the Asso river, first made in 1981 and only in chosen years since (the second in 1986): confirmed; its purchase is dated 1971 in one account and 1981 in others, so its place as the first vineyard is told as the estate tells it.

Tenuta Nuova's site: the estate's page gives the land where nobody had planted Sangiovese and the study of microclimates, clones, rootstocks and density, but no position; the trade puts its parcels in the south, Le Cetine near Sant'Angelo in Colle and Pietradonice near Castelnuovo dell'Abate. South east of the town was not confirmed and is cut.

The making: hand selection, an optical sorter (from 2017 by one merchant, with shorter macerations), spontaneous fermentation in conical steel for about twenty four days; oak given as 30, 35, 37 and 42 months by different merchants, in French tonneaux by several: about three years and the 600 litre size were changed.
The house rules: the founder and his son are described (people.json holds the son); the American magazine's ranking of the 2001 stays out; no price or score; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The founder: born in Treviso in 1937 (Gambero Rosso, Wikipedia; Vinous gives 1937 and a Milan upbringing), an insurance broker in Milan (Vinous, Decanter), died 16 February 2019 at eighty two (Decanter, Wikipedia): confirmed, so he is named with his dates.
The purchase of Case Basse in 1972: confirmed; the run down state rested on a writer's site and is cut.

The attack: the taps of the casks of the 2007 to 2012 vintages opened on the night of 2 December 2012 (Wikipedia; the night of 2 to 3 December by the family's statement), by a former employee: confirmed. The losses are given variously, so most of the wine stands.

The aftermath: producers and the consorzio offered wine of solidarity and he declined; English reports speak of his leaving or resigning in March 2013, Italian ones of an expulsion after a quarrel over a word: left is used. The founder's quoted reason for refusing rested on no source read and is cut.

The label: from the 2006 vintage, released in 2013, Toscana IGT rather than Brunello, a choice the estate calls commercial, for the identity of its wine, and the founder said the name Soldera would guarantee more than Brunello: confirmed. The estate's 2019 and 2021 sheets are headed Toscana IGP; the year of that change was not found.

The vineyards and the making: Case Basse and Intistieti, two plots of Sangiovese, at 320 metres by the estate; fermentation in large Slavonian oak vats of over 100 quintals after the berries are checked one by one; the 2019 sheet says the fermentation temperature is continuously monitored, so no temperature control is cut, with the six years in cask and the bottling without filtration, which rested on one citable source.

The garden: a botanical garden of over two hectares with antique roses, planted by the founder's wife, with nests and beehives among the rows: confirmed on the estate's page and the Italian botanical heritage guide.
Intistieti as a label of 1985 to 1992: not found, cut.
The house rules: the founder's widow and children and the former employee are not named; no price or score; British spelling; no dash.
